clue.text: See 10
Clue to tone of pudding

parts.note: read as wordplay, ETON put into a mess (jumbled) gives the word tone, so the answer is a clue that leads to tone

explanation.surface: A hint about the flavour of a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: the answer, read as an instruction (ETON, MESS it up), produces the word 'tone'. ETON MESS is a British dessert of strawberries, cream and broken meringue.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton mess is a classic English summer dessert of strawberries, meringue and cream.

clue.text: Basis of sweet course in times past: a lot of ale

indicators.note: the base or foundation of each word is taken as its opening letter here

parts.note: formerly, at one time, means once

explanation.surface: Musing on how a pudding course was built in the old days.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Basis of' takes the first letters of 'sweet' and 'course'.
explanation.definitionFit: A sconce was an old Oxford college forfeit of a large tankard of ale, and the mug itself.

clue.text: To make pudding, boil diced ingredients in empty tank

parts.note: a boil on the skin is a spot

indicators.note: the mixed letters go inside the emptied tank
an empty tank has its inside removed, leaving only the outer letters
the letters of diced are treated as ingredients to be mixed into a new order

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction for making a dessert with chopped components in a hollow vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'diced ingredients' reads as cookery but is a scramble of the word diced, which 'in' places inside the emptied tank. Spotted dick is a British steamed suet pudding with currants.
explanation.definitionFit: Spotted dick is a traditional British steamed suet pudding studded with dried fruit.

clue.text: Indulge in pudding (extra large)

indicators.note: the pudding gets an extra letter added into it

parts.note: pease pudding is a British dish of boiled split peas
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Ordering a supersized dessert as a treat.
explanation.walkthrough: PEASE pudding is a savoury British dish of boiled split peas; adding an extra L gives P-L-EASE.
explanation.definitionFit: To please someone is to gratify or humour them, a synonym of indulge.

clue.text: Spooner's starting to say joints are a problem with cold

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the opening sounds here change places
only the start of the word say is used

parts.note: knees are joints of the leg

explanation.surface: Someone claims aching joints come with catching a chill.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting to' takes S from 'say'; S followed by KNEES, with their opening sounds run together Spooner-fashion, is spoken as SNEEZE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sneezing is a typical symptom that comes with a head cold.

clue.text: They make cold scalp hot in a blizzard

definitions.text: They make cold scalp hot in a blizzard

parts.note: C is the abbreviation for cold, as on a tap

indicators.note: letters whirled about in a snowstorm are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Flat caps warm a chilly head when snow is swirling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a blizzard' scrambles C, SCALP and HOT; the whole clue also describes what the caps do.
explanation.definitionFit: Cloth caps are woollen flat caps that keep the head warm in cold weather.

clue.text: Banana split by Monsieur Escoffier, le premier pour préparer une bombe?

indicators.note: the banana is opened up and the abbreviation placed inside

parts.note: a plantain is a cooking banana

indicators.note: French for the first, so only the opening letter of Escoffier is used

explanation.surface: A Franglais menu note: Escoffier's banana split, perhaps a bombe-style dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split by' puts M inside PLANTAIN to give PLANTAMIN; 'le premier' adds E. Bombe here is French for a bomb, not the ice-cream dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: To plant a mine is to set an explosive device, which the French phrase describes.

clue.text: As it has no limit, no end of folly

definitions.text: As it has no limit, no end of folly

indicators.note: the letter is dropped from the word for something limitless

parts.note: infinity is the thing with no bound

indicators.note: an end of a word can be its opening letter, so the start of folly is taken

explanation.surface: Endless stupidity, like something that goes on for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'no' removes F, the letter at the 'end' (here the start) of 'folly', from the limitless word; the whole clue also describes boundless silliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Asininity is extreme silliness, behaving like an ass, so it is folly without bound.

clue.text: Pudding cooked ? I'll check with wife, say

parts.note: cooked in an oven means baked

indicators.note: the phrase spoken out loud gives a near-identical sound

parts.note: I'll ask her, checking with one's wife

explanation.surface: A cook unsure whether the dessert is done defers to a spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'say' signals a homophone: 'I'll ask her' is spoken like ALASKA. Baked Alaska is ice cream in meringue, briefly baked.
explanation.definitionFit: Baked Alaska is a dessert of ice cream and sponge covered in meringue and browned in the oven.

clue.text: See 17
Egg — perhaps pheasant — found by Lawrence

parts.note: pheasant is an example of game birds
T.E. Lawrence, Lawrence of Arabia, gives his initials

explanation.surface: A pheasant's egg discovered by a man called Lawrence.
explanation.walkthrough: T. E. Lawrence (of Arabia) is a common crossword source for TE.
explanation.definitionFit: A gamete is a reproductive cell, and an egg cell or ovum is one.

clue.text: Teaser: eg "oddities and whatnots"

indicators.note: the words are made odd, rearranged into a strange order

explanation.surface: A puzzle setter's example of curiosities and odd things.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddities' scrambles TEASER and EG. A whatnot is a stand of open shelves.
explanation.definitionFit: An étagère is a piece of furniture with open shelves, also called a whatnot.

clue.text: See 16
Boatman's in the way — it's deliberate

indicators.note: the setter is placed inside the street abbreviation

parts.note: ST is the abbreviation for street, a way
the setter Boatman is I, the 's being is

explanation.surface: The setter claims he gets in people's way on purpose.
explanation.walkthrough: Boatman is this puzzle's setter, so his name gives I.
explanation.definitionFit: A court or committee sits when it is in session to deliberate, so the verbs share a sense.

clue.text: Part of the story of English pastry is about the land

indicators.note: the pastry goes about, around, the land

parts.note: a pie is a pastry dish
sod is turf, the land

explanation.surface: A tale about English pastry being linked to the countryside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the pastry round the land, and English comes first; 'is' just links.
explanation.definitionFit: An episode is one instalment or incident within a longer narrative.

clue.text: Follow up point in game

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word is read from bottom to top

parts.note: to trace someone is to follow them
E is east, a compass point

explanation.surface: A follow-up point being made in a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' turns TRACE into ECART. Écarté is an old card game for two.
explanation.definitionFit: Écarté is a nineteenth-century French card game for two players.

clue.text: Ingredient of pudding: rat? Evidently, one says: "No thank you"

indicators.note: the answer is an ingredient within the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Someone, apparently a rat, is in the pudding and refusing thanks.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across 'pudding', 'rat' and 'Evidently'. The definition is cryptic: an ungrateful person withholds thanks.
explanation.definitionFit: An ingrate is an ungrateful person, one who fails to give thanks.

clue.text: See 4
Here nomads eat sheep's head for pudding

indicators.note: the place swallows the letter, taking it inside

parts.note: a desert is a place where nomads live

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Wandering herders dining on a sheep's head as a dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'head' gives S from 'sheep's', which 'eat' puts inside DESERT.
explanation.definitionFit: Dessert is the sweet course at the end of a meal, a pudding in British usage.

clue.text: Strange custom, to live in Devon

indicators.note: strange signals the letters are rearranged into an odd order

parts.note: to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: An unusual tradition followed by living in the West Country.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' scrambles CUSTOM into SUTCOM. Sutcombe is a village in Devon, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Sutcombe is a small village in the county of Devon, so it is a place found there.

clue.text: Sharp, concise facts: key on the Guardian

parts.note: info is the shortened form of information, facts
C is a musical key
the newspaper speaks of itself as us

explanation.surface: Brief, crisp facts as the key point of a newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Guardian is the paper this puzzle appears in, so it is US.
explanation.definitionFit: An image in focus is sharp, with crisp clear detail.

clue.text: One has faith in the UK's endless fishing? It contains the seeds of complete annihilation

definitions.text: One has faith in the UK

indicators.note: the shortened fishing word wraps round the other letters
the last letter is cut off

parts.note: angling is fishing with rod and line

indicators.note: a seed is where something starts, so the first letters are taken

explanation.surface: A believer in Britain pondering whether endless fishing heralds total ruin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' cuts ANGLING to ANGLIN; 'the seeds of' gives C and A, which 'contains' puts inside.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglican belongs to the Church of England, a believer within the UK's established church.

clue.text: Viz features Spooner's problem joint

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the starts here trade places

parts.note: lame, crippled, is a problem with a leg
a knee is a joint

explanation.surface: A magazine runs a piece about a bad knee.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spooner's' swaps the opening sounds of LAME KNEE to give NAME-LEE. Viz is also a British comic magazine, which the surface exploits.
explanation.definitionFit: Viz is short for videlicet, meaning that is to say, the same as namely.

clue.text: Folly of starting to let unhealthy nutrition affect chubby youths

indicators.note: only the start of each following word is used

explanation.surface: A warning that letting bad diet shape young people is foolish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starting to' takes the first letters of the six words from 'let' to 'youths'.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunacy is madness or extreme foolishness, a synonym for folly.

clue.text: Pudding for tea, say? Where's that?

definitions.text: Pudding for tea, say? Where's that?

parts.words: Pudding for tea, say? Where's that?
parts.note: the letter T, which sounds like tea, comes right ... in the alphabet, while the dessert course comes after the main

explanation.surface: Asking where dessert is at teatime.
explanation.walkthrough: Tea suggests the letter T, which sits after S in the alphabet. Afters is British slang for the dessert course.
explanation.definitionFit: Afters is informal British English for the pudding course that follows the main meal.

clue.text: Entice with an apple crumble

parts.note: an is the indefinite article, equivalent to a

indicators.note: the apple falls to pieces and its letters are remade

explanation.surface: Tempting someone with a fruit dessert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crumble' scrambles A and APPLE; apple crumble is also a pudding, which suits the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To appeal to someone is to attract or tempt them, which is what enticing does.

clue.text: Agitated and drunk after end of dinner

indicators.note: the drunk word comes after the letter from dinner
only the final letter of dinner is used

parts.note: oiled is slang for drunk

explanation.surface: Someone flustered and tipsy once the meal is over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'end of' takes R from 'dinner', and 'after' puts OILED behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: Roiled means stirred up or disturbed, the same as agitated.

clue.text: See 8
Police duo outlook?

annotationWithheld.why: Police duo outlook? (4,5): the anagram of POLICE DUO is signalled by 'out' and defined by 'look', both inside the single word 'outlook', so one word does two jobs

clue.text: Pudding could be said to anticipate shortage

indicators.note: to anticipate is to come before, so the letter precedes the next word
spoken out loud, the word be sounds like the letter B

parts.note: the word be is taken as spoken
a shortage is a lack

explanation.surface: A dessert might be called a sign that supplies will run short.
explanation.walkthrough: The spoken word 'be' gives B, which 'to anticipate' places before LACK. Black pudding is a British blood sausage, savoury despite the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Black pudding is a British blood sausage, so black names a kind of pudding.

clue.text: Barge recklessly overloaded with pudding ingredient, a root

indicators.note: the barge carries a load of suet around it, so suet surrounds it

parts.note: suet is beef fat used in steamed puddings

indicators.note: the barge is handled recklessly, so its letters are tossed about

explanation.surface: A carelessly overloaded boat full of pudding fat, and a root vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'recklessly' scrambles the barge into GARBE, and 'overloaded with' wraps the fatty pudding ingredient round it.
explanation.definitionFit: Sugar beet is a plant grown for its root, from which sugar is extracted.
